evidence.title: Research on Security Enhancement Methods for Adversarial Robust Large Language Model Intelligent Agents for Medical Decision-Making Tasks
evidence.outcome: Effect of removing input risk perception module on accuracy and attack success rate
evidence.effect: Removing risk perception reduced accuracy by 6.7% and increased attack success rate by 13.8% in ablation.
evidence.quote: Ablation experiments quantify each module's contribution: removing risk perception, evidence retrieval, consistency verification, and confidence reweighting reduces accuracy by 6.7%, 9.1%, 7.6%, and 4.4%, respectively, and increases attack success rate by 13.8%, 11.1%, 8.6%, and 6.9%.

evidence.title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Attack success rates under adversarial testing, secured vs insecure agent workflow
evidence.effect: Across 500 attack scenarios, mean ASR dropped for RAG poisoning (31% to 10%) and data-field injection (42% to 25%); network injection eliminated.
evidence.quote: The TRiSM-guided agentic workflow reduced mean attack success rates from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection, while eliminating the network injection vector entirely through server-side prompt construction.

evidence.title: Removing Adversarial Noise in X-ray Images via Total Variation Minimization and Patch-Based Regularization for Robust Deep Learning-based Diagnosis
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Classifier accuracy under FGSM adversarial attack, before and after total variation denoising
evidence.effect: Average accuracy fell from 95.56% to 19.83% under adversarial attack; after denoising it rose from 19.83% to 88.23% on adversarial images.
evidence.quote: Post-denoising, the model exhibits a remarkable accuracy improvement, surging from 19.83 to 88.23% on adversarial images.

evidence.title: Auto encoder-based defense mechanism against popular adversarial attacks in deep learning
evidence.outcome: Pneumonia classifier accuracy under FGSM/PGD adversarial attacks with and without autoencoder denoising defense
evidence.effect: PGD attack cut overall accuracy by up to 67% on VGG16; the autoencoder improved accuracy by up to 16% against PGD attacks in VGG16 and VGG19.
evidence.quote: The autoencoder improves accuracy by up to 16% against PGD attacks in both the VGG16 and VGG19 models.

evidence.title: Robustness of a Large Language Model (LLM)-Based Virtual Patient for Japanese History-Taking Training Under Direct and Indirect Instructional Contamination
evidence.outcome: Robustness to adversarial contaminated inputs with input sanitization defense
evidence.effect: Direct contamination collapsed fidelity to 0.098 (hit rate 0.077); input sanitizer restored fidelity to 0.945 and hit rate to 0.942 without refusals.
evidence.quote: Under direct contamination, case fidelity improved from 0.098 to 0.945, and turn-target hit rate improved from 0.077 to 0.942 after defense.

evidence.title: Federated TinyML and digital twin framework for secure and resilient IoMT-based ICU monitoring
evidence.outcome: Critical-class recall under label-flipping poisoning attack, PBF versus FedAvg, Krum, Trimmed Mean, Coordinate Median
evidence.effect: Under a targeted label-flipping attack, PBF achieved 86.79% accuracy and 0.904 critical-class recall; PBF gave stronger protection of critical-class recall than the comparison aggregation methods.

evidence.title: Data Poisoning Vulnerabilities Across Healthcare AI Architectures: A Security Threat Analysis
evidence.outcome: Success rate and detection time of data poisoning attacks on healthcare AI
evidence.effect: Attackers with 100-500 poisoned samples compromised healthcare AI regardless of dataset size, often over 60 percent success; detection estimated at 6 to 12 months or not at all.
evidence.quote: Our findings indicate that attackers with access to only 100-500 samples can compromise healthcare AI regardless of dataset size, often achieving over 60 percent success, with detection taking an estimated 6 to 12 months or sometimes not occurring at all.

evidence.title: Many-to-One Adversarial Consensus: Exposing Multi-Agent Collusion Risks in AI-Based Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Attack success and harmful recommendation rates under colluding adversarial assistant agents
evidence.effect: Collusion drives Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Harmful Recommendation Rates (HRR) up to 100% in unprotected systems.
evidence.quote: Using 50 representative clinical questions, we find that collusion drives the Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Harmful Recommendation Rates (HRR) up to 100% in unprotected systems.

evidence.title: Silent Manipulation of Mental Health Treatment Recommendations from a Large Language Model
evidence.outcome: Shift in medication-versus-self-care balance of depression advice under inference-time activation steering
evidence.effect: Medication-versus-self-care balance declined 0.32 per unit of steering amplitude (95% CI, -0.39 to -0.25; P<.001); largest shift (β=-0.44) in scenarios with no stated treatment preference; clinician referral unchanged (P=.63).
evidence.quote: Across 372 generations, steering produced a graded, dose-dependent shift in the medication-versus-self-care balance, which declined by 0.32 per unit of amplitude (β = −0.32; 95% CI, −0.39 to −0.25; P < .001); medication extent fell and self-care extent rose.

commentary.bottom_line: Seven studies test specific defenses such as input sanitization, image denoising, secured agent workflows, and poisoning-resistant aggregation, and each reports lower attack success or recovered accuracy in offline benchmarks. No study tests an organizational red-teaming program in a deployed clinical system, so the evidence that the practice as a whole prevents patient harm is very low.

perspectives.view: All seven tests are level 5 automated benchmarks or offline simulations, most without a reported setting or sample size. Each evaluates one technical defense against attacks the authors built, not routine red-teaming by a health system. The results agree in direction, but indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

Injected inputs produced unsafe pregnancy drug advice in 91.7% of extreme-harm scenarios, and poisoning detection was estimated at 6 to 12 months or never. Defenses reduced but did not remove risk. RAG poisoning success fell from 31% to 10%, and median aggregation gave inconsistent benefit at 10% noise.

No defense was tested inside a live clinical workflow, and none of the studies reports staff time or alert burden. One input sanitizer restored fidelity from 0.098 to 0.945 without refusals, which suggests some defenses may avoid blocking legitimate use. A secured agent workflow tested 500 attack scenarios offline only.

A backdoor aimed at one demographic group took hold after 2.6% of training labels were flipped, and five detectors failed to find it. This suggests poisoning can target specific populations. The only defense test involving non-English input used Japanese text in Japan, and no test examined Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled devices lists malformed input (fuzz) testing, and FUTURE-AI calls for regular evaluation of attack defenses. No supplied study measures whether meeting these expectations lowers attack success in practice. The recommendation therefore rests on expert consensus and benchmark evidence rather than on tests of compliance programs.

One study built a distilled surrogate model for $12, and it produced unsafe completions for 86% of adversarial prompts. That figure suggests attacks cost attackers little. None of the defense studies reports what red-teaming, input validation, or data provenance controls cost a health system in staff or tooling, so budgeting cannot yet draw on evidence.

Models given fabricated clinical details produced false lab values or nonexistent conditions in 50% to 82.7% of cases. Patients could receive such outputs without knowing that an input was manipulated. No study measured whether adversarial testing changed what patients actually received or how easily they could reach a clinician to check.

commentary.research_gap: No study evaluates a recurring red-teaming and input-validation program in a deployed health care AI system. Needed work would compare sites with and without such programs on attacks detected, time to detection, unsafe outputs reaching clinicians or patients, and staff and vendor cost. Defense tests should use realistic clinical inputs and report setting and sample size.
commentary.underserved_note: One defense test (pmid:42326139) used non-English (Japanese) input in Japan. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, and no test reported results by patient subgroup. A hazard study showing a demographic backdoor that evaded five detectors suggests that defenses validated on general benchmarks may not protect specific groups, and this remains untested.
